listening.title: Campus Bicycle-Repair Desk
listening.focus: Everyday service details: problem, place, price and time
listening.script:
STAFF: Good morning, Campus Bicycle-Repair Desk, this is Daniel speaking. How can I help you today?
STUDENT: Hi, I'm Anna, a first-year student. My bike has a flat back tyre, and the brakes feel loose. Can I leave it here for repair?
STAFF: Of course, Anna. We can fix both problems here at the desk. Could you please write your full name on this repair form?
STUDENT: Yes. It's Anna Lopez, L-O-P-E-Z.
STAFF: Thanks very much, Anna. And can I take your phone number?
STUDENT: Yes, it's 07715 482390.
STAFF: Thanks. And what type of bike is it exactly?
STUDENT: It's a blue city bike, quite old. I use it every day to come to college.
STAFF: Okay. You can leave it in our storage room. Go down the hall, past the sports office, and it's Room 4.
STUDENT: Sorry, did you say Room 3?
STAFF: No, Room 4 — sorry, I know the sign on the door still says Room 3, but we moved last week. It's Room 4 now.
STUDENT: Got it, Room 4. How much will the repair cost in total?
STAFF: A flat tyre repair is 8 pounds, and fixing the brakes is 6 pounds. So 14 pounds in total. Our desk is open from 9 to 5 on weekdays, and you can pay when you collect the bike.
STUDENT: That's fine. How long will it take exactly?
STAFF: Normally two days. If you leave it today, Monday, it will be ready on Wednesday afternoon. Actually, wait — Wednesday is a holiday, so the desk is closed. It will be ready on Thursday morning after 10 o'clock.
STUDENT: Thursday after 10, okay. Do I need to bring anything when I collect it?
STAFF: Yes, please bring the yellow receipt I will give you now, and pay by card. We don't take cash anymore because the card machine is faster.
STUDENT: Okay, yellow receipt and pay by card. Thank you very much for your help.
STAFF: You're welcome. See you on Thursday morning.

reading.title: A Student Project About Local Trees
reading.focus: Main ideas, details, and claims in a student project
reading.passage:
Maya and Tom are second-year college students studying the environment. Last spring, they started a small project about the trees in Greenfield Park, a large public park near their college. They wanted to answer a simple question: what kinds of trees grow in the park, and how do people use the shade from those trees?
To begin, they chose three walking paths in different parts of the park: one near the lake, one near the playground, and one near the main entrance. Every Saturday morning for six weeks, they walked each path and counted the trees. They took photos of leaves and bark, measured the width of the trunks with a tape, and wrote notes about the height and shape of each tree. They also checked an old park map from the library, but they did not copy it because some trees had been cut down or newly planted.
After six weeks, they had records for 180 trees. Their main finding was clear: maple trees were the most common, with 90 trees, or half of the total. Oak trees were second, with 40 trees. The rest were a mix of pine, birch, and small fruit trees. Most of the fruit trees were near the playground, and a park worker told them that local families had planted those trees five years ago to make the area nicer.
One large oak tree near the lake was a good example of the old trees in the park. Maya measured its trunk at 2 metres wide, and Tom estimated it was more than 80 years old. They took several photos of its wide branches and thick leaves. The students liked this tree, but they did not say it was the most important tree in the park. It was only one example in their notes.
The students' main claim was about shade and park use. On hot afternoons, they counted people sitting under trees and people sitting in sunny places. They found about three times more people in shady areas. From this, they claimed that shade from trees helps people enjoy the park for longer in summer. They wrote that shade is not just nice to look at; it changes how people use the park.
In their final report, Maya and Tom suggested planting ten more maple trees near the playground, where there is little shade. They will present their results to the park office next month and ask if student volunteers can help with the planting.

writingPrompts.focus: Clear main ideas and direct comparison from a simple table
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the number of stalls at Green Lane Neighbourhood Food Market in 2020 and 2025.

In 2020: Fresh fruit - 12 stalls, Fresh vegetables - 15 stalls, Bread and cakes - 8 stalls, Hot drinks and juices - 6 stalls. Total - 41 stalls.
In 2025: Fresh fruit - 18 stalls, Fresh vegetables - 20 stalls, Bread and cakes - 10 stalls, Hot drinks and juices - 12 stalls. Total - 60 stalls.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

writingPrompts.focus: Accurate simple description of a weekly timetable
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the weekly timetable of a student study group at Parkside Library in March 2026.

Monday 16:00-17:30: Maths problem practice, 6 students
Tuesday 16:00-17:00: English reading, 8 students
Wednesday 16:00-17:30: Science homework, 5 students
Thursday 16:00-17:00: English writing, 7 students
Friday 16:00-17:00: Music club review and weekly test preparation, 10 students

All sessions are led by two older student helpers. Friday has the highest attendance.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Local Food Markets and Supermarkets
writingPrompts.focus: Clear opinion with direct everyday evidence
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people prefer to buy food at a small neighbourhood food market, while others prefer to buy food at a large supermarket.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

writingPrompts.focus: Simple comparison with familiar academic examples
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some students like to study alone at home, while others like to join a study group with a fixed weekly timetable.

Do the advantages of studying in a group outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Community Music Clubs for Young People
writingPrompts.focus: Clear ideas and simple explanation of benefits
writingPrompts.prompt:
In many towns, a community music club meets once a week so young people can learn an instrument, sing, and play together.

Some people think local councils should give more money to support these clubs. Others think young people can learn music by themselves online.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

speakingPrompts.focus: Familiar everyday answers about food shopping
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions. Give short, clear answers with one or two reasons or examples.
1. Where do you usually buy your food?
2. How often do you visit a local food market?
3. What kind of fresh food do you like most?
4. Do you like cooking at home or eating outside? Why?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 1 · Study Habits and Free Time
speakingPrompts.focus: Simple personal answers about study and music
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions. Give short, clear answers with one or two reasons or examples.
1. Do you prefer to study in the morning or in the evening? Why?
2. Do you usually study alone or with friends?
3. Do you enjoy listening to music while you study?
4. What do you usually do after your study time finishes?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card - A Visit to a Neighbourhood Food Market
speakingPrompts.focus: Clear description of a familiar event with explanation
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a visit you made to a neighbourhood food market. You should say:
• where the market was and when you went there
• who you went with
• what you saw, heard, or bought there
• and explain why you remember this visit.

You have one minute to prepare. Then speak for one to two minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Local Markets and Community Life
speakingPrompts.focus: Giving reasons and simple evaluation about local shops
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Discuss the following ideas. Give reasons and compare ideas, not only facts from memory.
1. Why do some people prefer small food markets to large supermarkets?
2. How can neighbourhood markets help the local community?
3. Do you think online food shopping will replace local markets in the future? Why or why not?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Music Clubs and Learning Together
speakingPrompts.focus: Explaining benefits and evaluating group learning
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Discuss the following ideas. Give reasons and compare ideas, not only facts from memory.
1. What are the benefits of joining a community music club for young people?
2. Is it better to learn music in a group or alone? Why?
3. Should schools give more time for group activities like music and study groups? Why or why not?
